docs.title: airflow3-dag-gen
docs.text:
Generate Apache Airflow 3 DAGs from a single canonical YAML config using a Go-based generator.

Requires Apache Airflow 3.2.2+. This project targets the Airflow 3.x SDK and provider package layout; it is not compatible with Airflow 2.x.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Single config — define DAGs once in config/projects/<project>/dags.yaml
  • Per-environment support — enable/disable DAGs and tasks per env (dev/staging/prod); override params and default_args per env with _env blocks
  • Multi-project — one repo holds configs for many Airflow projects, each in its own sub-directory
  • Airflow 3 Assets (3.0+) — declare Asset outlets and inlets on any task; enables data-aware DAG scheduling
  • Dynamic task mapping (3.0+) — .partial().expand() and .partial().expand_kwargs() generated from YAML; map_index_template supported
  • DAG display name (3.2+) — set a human-readable display name independent of the DAG ID via dag_display_name
  • Standard provider paths (3.0+) — generated imports use airflow.providers.standard.* and airflow.sdk; no legacy airflow.operators.* paths
  • Flexible output — copy DAGs to a local directory or bake them into a Docker image
  • Syntax validation — every generated .py file is validated with python3 -m py_compile before reporting success
  • Makefile — all developer actions via make
  • Environment taxonomy — define named environments with an optional class (production, staging, non-production) in settings.yaml; built-in defaults for prd/prod/stg/staging/dev
  • Fine-grained env scoping — enabled_envs whitelist (DAG only generated for these named environments) and enabled_classes whitelist (DAG only generated when the active env belongs to this class); ideal for non-prod-only validation/mock DAGs
  • DAG-level _env overrides — override schedule, catchup, max_active_runs, or tags per environment at the DAG level (previously only params and default_args supported _env)
  • dag_instances list — stamp N DAGs from one template in a compact list; avoids repeating identical DAG blocks with template:
  • Parallel generation — goroutine worker pool for concurrent py_compile validation; ~8× faster at 1000+ DAG scale
  • Incremental generation — --incremental flag caches SHA-256 of each rendered file; unchanged DAGs are skipped in subsequent runs
  • DAG manifest — --manifest flag writes manifest.json to the output directory listing every generated DAG with its metadata
  • Naming convention linter — config/linting.yaml defines regex rules for DAG/task IDs, required tags, and description presence; make lint-dags and make check enforce them in CI
  • Promote --apply — promote.py --apply prints (or --output FILE writes) the minimal _env.{to_env} YAML patch to make two environments converge

docs.title: Why af3-dag-builder over Astro DAG Factory?
docs.text:
Astro DAG Factory lets you define Airflow DAGs in YAML — but it works by loading and evaluating that YAML inside the Airflow scheduler at parse time. Every scheduler heartbeat re-parses your YAML files and rebuilds DAG objects in memory. af3-dag-builder takes the opposite approach: it is a compile-time code generator that produces static Python .py files you review, commit, and deploy like any other code.

af3-dag-builder Astro DAG Factory How it works Go binary generates static .py files Python library builds DAGs in-memory at parse time Airflow 3 native Built for Airflow 3 from the ground up Built for Airflow 2; Airflow 3 support is incomplete Scheduler overhead None — DAGs are already Python files YAML parsed on every scheduler scan cycle Reviewable output Real .py files in git, diffable and auditable No generated files; DAG code is never visible Syntax validation python3 -m py_compile on every file before deploy No pre-deployment validation Multi-environment First-class _env overrides; per-env enable/disable No built-in environment promotion model Secret detection Built-in lint_secrets.py blocks hardcoded secrets Not provided Operator governance Central registry.yaml; unknown operators fail CI No operator registry Dynamic task mapping Native .expand() / .expand_kwargs() support Not supported for Airflow 3 Airflow 3 Assets Native Asset inlet/outlet declarations Not supported Reuse patterns DAG templates + task library Not provided Promotion diff scripts/promote.py shows staging→prod delta Not provided Parallel generation Worker pool; py_compile runs in parallel (~8× faster at scale) Python interpreter (serial) Incremental generation --incremental skips files with unchanged content hash Full regeneration every time DAG manifest --manifest → manifest.json with per-DAG metadata Not provided Naming convention linter config/linting.yaml with regex + tag rules; CI gate Not provided Promote --apply promote.py --apply prints _env patch to close env gap Not provided Non-prod-only DAGs enabled_classes: [non-production] limits DAG to dev/staging class Not provided Generator speed Compiled Go binary Python (interpreted at runtime)

The core trade-off: DAG Factory is a lighter drop-in for existing Airflow 2 deployments — if you already run Python DAGs and want a quick YAML abstraction, it works. af3-dag-builder is the right choice when you want Airflow 3 semantics, CI-gated validation, environment promotion discipline, and generated files that your team can read, review, and audit exactly like handwritten code.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# 1. Build the Go generator
make build-go

# 2. Validate your config
make validate

# 3. Generate DAGs (dev environment, local output)
make generate

# 4. Inspect output
ls output/dags/

# 5. Smoke-test with local Airflow 3
make airflow-up
# → http://localhost:8080  (admin / admin)
make airflow-down

docker-compose.yml ships a placeholder AIRFLOW_JWT_SECRET default for local use only. To override it, copy .env.example to .env (gitignored) and set a real value — never commit actual secrets.

docs.title: config/projects/<name>/dags.yaml
docs.text:
name: my_project

custom_operators:
  - name: MyOp
    import_path: "plugins.my_module.MyOp"

dags:
  - id: my_dag
    schedule: "@daily"
    start_date: "2024-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [example]

    enabled:          # per-environment enabled flags
      dev: true
      prod: false

    enabled_envs: [dev, staging]   # whitelist: only generated for these env names
    # OR:
    enabled_classes: [non-production]  # whitelist: only when env class matches

    _env:                 # DAG-level per-env overrides (schedule, catchup, max_active_runs, tags)
      prod:
        schedule: "0 4 * * *"
        max_active_runs: 2

    default_args:
      owner: my_team
      retries: 1
      retry_delay_minutes: 5
      email_on_failure: false
      _env:           # env-specific overrides
        prod:
          retries: 3

    tasks:
      - id: say_hello
        operator: BashOperator
        params:
          bash_command: "echo dev"
          _env:
            prod:
              bash_command: "echo prod"
      - id: process
        operator: PythonOperator
        enabled:
          prod: false
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.my_project.process"
        dependencies: [say_hello]

docs.title: Environment Resolution Rules
docs.text:
1. dag.enabled_envs set and env not in list → DAG skipped entirely
  2. dag.enabled_classes set and env class not in list → DAG skipped entirely
  3. dag.enabled[env] == false → DAG skipped entirely
  4. task.enabled[env] == false → task omitted; downstream deps cleaned up
  5. params._env[env] → merged onto base params; _env key removed
  6. default_args._env[env] → same merge applied to default_args

docs.title: Airflow 3 Features
docs.text:
Dynamic task mapping (requires Airflow 3.0+) 

- id: process_item
  operator: PythonOperator
  params:
    python_callable: "dags.pipeline.process"
  dynamic_map:
    expand:
      item: "{{ get_items.output }}"
    map_index_template: "item_{{ ti.map_index }}"
  dependencies: [get_items]

Asset outlets (requires Airflow 3.0+) 

- id: produce_data
  operator: PythonOperator
  params:
    python_callable: "dags.pipeline.produce"
  datasets:
    outlets:
      - uri: "s3://bucket/path"

DAG display name (requires Airflow 3.2+) 

- id: my_dag_v2
  dag_display_name: "My Pipeline (v2)"
  schedule: "@daily"
  ...

Custom operators: 

custom_operators:
  - name: MyOp
    import_path: "plugins.my_module.MyOp"

tasks:
  - id: run_custom
    operator: MyOp
    params:
      my_param: "value"

docs.title: Pre-commit hook
docs.text:
A hook in scripts/pre-commit automatically runs the full test suite before every git commit. Install it once:

make install-hooks

After installation, any commit that would break a test is blocked with a clear error. Bypass in exceptional cases with git commit --no-verify.

docs.title: Adding a New Project
docs.text:
1. Create a directory under config/projects/<project_name>/
  2. Add a dags.yaml (or defaults.yaml + per-domain files — see config/projects/project_b/ for an example)
  3. Run make validate to confirm the config is valid
  4. Run make generate to produce the DAG files

docs.title: Custom Operators
docs.text:
1. Copy config/plugins/my_operator.py → plugins/<your_operator>.py in your Airflow deployment
  2. Register in custom_operators in your project's dags.yaml
  3. Use the operator name in task definitions

docs.title: Generator
docs.text: A standalone Go binary (app/dagGen/) reads the canonical YAML, resolves environment overrides, and renders Python DAG files from text/template templates. Produces one .py file per DAG.

docs.title: 5.1 Go generator pipeline
docs.text:
main.go
  │
  ├── config/loader.go
  │     LoadSettings()        ← config/settings.yaml  (+ environments block)
  │     LoadLintRules()       ← config/linting.yaml   (optional)
  │     DiscoverProjects()    ← config/projects/*/
  │     LoadProject()         ← dags.yaml / defaults.yaml + extra *.yaml files
  │                              expandDAGInstances()  ← dag_instances → DAG structs
  │
  ├── env/resolver.go
  │     Resolve()             ← filters by enabled_envs, enabled_classes, enabled map
  │     resolveDAGFields()    ← DAG-level _env overrides (schedule, catchup, etc.)
  │     ResolveTasks()        ← filters disabled tasks, cleans dep edges
  │     resolveDefaultArgs()  ← merges _env overrides into default_args
  │     MergeParams()         ← merges _env overrides into task params
  │
  ├── linter/linter.go
  │     Lint()                ← checks dag_id/task_id patterns, required tags, description
  │
  ├── generator/dag.go
  │     Generate()            ← Phase 1: render all DAGs (serial)
  │                              Phase 2: write via goroutine pool (parallel py_compile)
  │     renderDAG()           ← builds DAGRenderData, executes template
  │     buildTaskRenderData() ← builds TaskRenderData slice
  │     collectCallbackImports() ← resolves callback import statements
  │
  ├── generator/manifest.go
  │     BuildManifest()       ← resolves env + builds Manifest struct → manifest.json
  │
  ├── generator/operator.go
  │     ResolveImports()      ← deduped import statements for all operators
  │     ResolveClass()        ← class name for template (last path segment)
  │
  ├── generator/template.go
  │     TemplateFuncs()       ← pythonBool, pythonValue, pyStr, etc.
  │
  ├── templates/dag.py.tmpl   ← Go text/template → Python source
  │
  └── output/local.go | output/image.go
        Write()               ← writes .py, validates with py_compile (parallel)
        Flush()               ← saves incremental hash cache (.daggen-cache.json)

Key design choice: the template receives DAGRenderData — a plain Go struct with no methods. All logic lives in Go; the template is pure presentation. This keeps the template readable and keeps business logic testable.

docs.title: 5.2 Environment resolution
docs.text:
Resolution happens after preprocessing (defaults → task library → templates) and before rendering. The key invariant: the resolved struct contains no _env keys and no disabled items.

Input DAG (raw from YAML)
  │
  ├── dag.enabled_envs set and env not in list?     →  skip entirely (return false)
  │
  ├── dag.enabled_classes set and envClass not in list?  →  skip entirely (return false)
  │
  ├── dag.enabled[env] == false?  →  skip entirely (return false)
  │
  ├── resolveDAGFields(dag, env)
  │     apply _env[env] overrides: schedule, catchup, max_active_runs, tags
  │
  ├── resolveDefaultArgs(dag.DefaultArgs, env)
  │     merge _env[env] fields into base, nil out EnvOverrides
  │
  └── ResolveTasks(dag.Tasks, env)
        for each task:
          isEnabled(task.Enabled, env) == false?  →  add to disabled set
        for each non-disabled task:
          MergeParams(task.Params, env)           →  merge _env, remove _env key
          filterDeps(task.Dependencies, disabled) →  remove edges to disabled tasks
          task.Enabled = nil

Go: app/dagGen/internal/env/resolver.go

docs.title: 5.3 Template rendering
docs.text:
The DAG template (app/dagGen/templates/dag.py.tmpl) is a standard Go text/template. It is embedded via go:embed in templates/embed.go and read at runtime.

Key template conventions: - {{- action }} trims all whitespace/newlines before the action - {{ action -}} trims all whitespace/newlines after the action - Optional fields use {{- if .Field }}...{{- end }} — omitted when zero value - *bool fields use the boolPtrRendered helper (returns "" for nil → skipped by {{with}}) - All string-to-Python conversions go through pyStr (quoted) or pythonValue (type-aware)

docs.title: 6.1 Adding a new YAML field
docs.text:
Changes must be made in all four places — schema, types, resolver (if env-overridable), generator, and template.

Example: adding retries_exponential_backoff: bool to tasks.

1. JSON Schema (config/schema/dags.schema.json) — add to the task definition:

"retries_exponential_backoff": {
  "type": "boolean",
  "description": "Use exponential backoff between retries instead of fixed delay"
}

2. Go types (app/dagGen/internal/config/types.go) — add to Task:

RetriesExponentialBackoff bool `yaml:"retries_exponential_backoff,omitempty"`

3. Render data (app/dagGen/internal/generator/dag.go) — add to TaskRenderData:

RetriesExponentialBackoff bool

Populate it in buildTaskRenderData():

result[i] = TaskRenderData{
    ...
    RetriesExponentialBackoff: t.RetriesExponentialBackoff,
}

4. Template (app/dagGen/templates/dag.py.tmpl) — add inside the Operator(...) constructor:

{{- if .RetriesExponentialBackoff }}
        retries_exponential_backoff=True,
{{- end }}

5. Tests — add a Go test in dag_test.go.

docs.title: 6.2 Adding a standard operator
docs.text:
Standard operators are registered in the Go generator (app/dagGen/internal/generator/operator.go):

var standardOperators = map[string]string{
    ...
    "S3KeySensor": "from airflow.providers.amazon.aws.sensors.s3 import S3KeySensor",
}

Update the standard operator table in docs/userguide/custom-operators.md and docs/onboarding.md.

docs.title: 6.3 Modifying the DAG template
docs.text:
The template is at app/dagGen/templates/dag.py.tmpl. It is embedded at compile time — no separate copy step needed.

Whitespace control is critical in Python output. Use {{- and -}} to eliminate unintended blank lines. Run make generate && python3 -m py_compile output/dags/*.py after any template change.

Testing template output — write a table-driven test in dag_test.go that creates a minimal config.DAG, calls renderDAG, and asserts on specific substrings in the output:

func TestMyNewField(t *testing.T) {
    dag := config.DAG{
        ID: "test_dag", Schedule: "@daily", StartDate: "2024-01-01",
        MyNewField: "expected_value",
        Tasks: []config.Task{{ID: "t1", Operator: "EmptyOperator"}},
    }
    project := &config.ProjectConfig{Name: "proj", DAGs: []config.DAG{dag}}
    settings := &config.Settings{Environment: "dev"}

    var w mockOutputHandler
    if err := Generate([]*config.ProjectConfig{project}, settings, &w); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if !strings.Contains(w.files["test_dag"], "expected_value") {
        t.Errorf("expected 'expected_value' in output:\n%s", w.files["test_dag"])
    }
}

docs.title: 6.4 Extending environment resolution
docs.text:
When adding a new field that should be env-overridable (like an existing _env field):

Go — add to DefaultArgsOverride (for default_args fields) or handle in MergeParams (for task params, which already handles any key generically).

For a completely new override section, follow the pattern in resolveDefaultArgs:

func resolveDefaultArgs(da config.DefaultArgs, env string) config.DefaultArgs {
    ...
    if ov.MyNewField != nil {
        da.MyNewField = *ov.MyNewField
    }
    ...
}

Task-level params already use generic map merging (MergeParams) so no changes are needed there for new task param fields.

docs.title: 6.5 Adding a template function
docs.text:
Template functions live in app/dagGen/internal/generator/template.go. Register them in TemplateFuncs():

func TemplateFuncs() template.FuncMap {
    return template.FuncMap{
        ...
        "myNewFunc": myNewFunc,
    }
}

func myNewFunc(input string) string {
    return strings.ToUpper(input)
}

Then use in the template: {{ .MyField | myNewFunc }}

Write a unit test alongside the function. Keep functions pure and side-effect-free.

docs.title: 6.6 Adding a linting rule
docs.text:
Linting rules are pure data — no code change needed for most additions. Edit config/linting.yaml:

rules:
  dag_id:
    pattern: "^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$"
    message: "DAG IDs must be lowercase snake_case"
  required_tags:
    - team
    - domain
  description_required: true

To add a new rule type (e.g. check that schedule matches a pattern):

  1. Add a field to LintRuleSet in app/dagGen/internal/config/linting.go
  2. Add a field to LintRules.Rules if needed
  3. Add the check in Lint() in app/dagGen/internal/linter/linter.go
  4. Add a test in linter_test.go

The linter is always bypassed when config/linting.yaml does not exist.

docs.title: Go tests
docs.text:
Follow the existing table-driven pattern. Use mockOutputHandler from dag_test.go to capture output without writing files:

type mockOutputHandler struct {
    files map[string]string
}
func (m *mockOutputHandler) Write(dagID, group, content string) error {
    if m.files == nil { m.files = make(map[string]string) }
    m.files[dagID] = content
    return nil
}

Test naming: Test<Package>_<Scenario> — e.g., TestResolver_DisabledTaskDepsRemoved, TestGenerate_TriggerRuleRendered.

Coverage requirements: - Every new field added to types.go needs at least one renderer test in dag_test.go - Every change to resolver.go needs a resolution test in resolver_test.go - Operator resolution changes need tests in operator_test.go

docs.title: 8. Code style and linting
docs.text:
make lint       # runs golangci-lint

Go: - Standard gofmt formatting (enforced by golangci-lint) - No panic in library code — return errors - Error messages: lowercase, no trailing punctuation - Use fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err) for error wrapping

Comments: - Write comments only when the why is non-obvious - No doc comments restating what the function name already says - Mark intentional design constraints with a short inline comment

docs.title: 9. Schema versioning
docs.text:
The schema version ("1.0") is validated in app/dagGen/internal/config/loader.go:

const CurrentSchemaVersion = "1.0"

When to bump the version:

Change type Action New optional field No bump — backwards compatible Removed field Bump to "2.0" Renamed field Bump to "2.0" Changed field type Bump to "2.0" New required field Bump to "2.0"

When bumping: 1. Change CurrentSchemaVersion in loader.go 2. Update the version pattern in dags.schema.json if needed 3. Update all version: "1.0" lines in config/projects/ 4. Add a migration note in this file

docs.title: 10. Keeping docs/userguide/ current
docs.text:
Field reference tables in docs/userguide/yaml-reference.md and docs/userguide/custom-operators.md are auto-generated from the JSON schema and operator.go. Never edit them by hand — your changes will be overwritten on the next make docs run.

When you add or change a field:

# 1. Update the schema (add/edit the property + its description)
#    config/schema/dags.schema.json

# 2. Regenerate the guide
make docs

# 3. Commit both files together
git add config/schema/dags.schema.json docs/userguide/yaml-reference.md

Sections generated automatically (marked with <!-- generated:X --> / <!-- /generated:X -->): - DAG fields table (docs/userguide/yaml-reference.md) — from schema.definitions.dag - Task fields table (docs/userguide/yaml-reference.md) — from schema.definitions.task - trigger_rule values table (docs/userguide/yaml-reference.md) — from schema.definitions.task.properties.trigger_rule.enum - default_args fields table (docs/userguide/yaml-reference.md) — from schema.definitions.default_args - Standard operators table (docs/userguide/custom-operators.md) — from app/dagGen/internal/generator/operator.go

Sections maintained by hand (everything else — narrative, examples, FAQ, headings).

CI gate: make check runs python scripts/generate_docs.py --check and fails if the guide is stale. You will see a unified diff showing exactly what changed in the schema but was not regenerated into the guide.

Adding per-value descriptions to trigger_rule or weight_rule: these are stored in the TRIGGER_RULE_DESCRIPTIONS dict in scripts/generate_docs.py (JSON Schema draft-7 has no per-enum-value metadata). Update the dict there.

docs.title: 11. Pull request checklist
docs.text:
Before opening a PR, confirm:

  • [ ] make test passes (Go unit tests)
  • [ ] make lint passes (no golangci-lint errors)
  • [ ] make validate passes against the existing project configs
  • [ ] New fields are added to all relevant locations: schema, Go types, Go renderer, Go template
  • [ ] New fields have tests in dag_test.go
  • [ ] docs/userguide/ is updated with any new user-facing fields or behaviours
  • [ ] Standard operator additions are documented in the operator table in docs/userguide/custom-operators.md and docs/onboarding.md
  • [ ] No hardcoded secrets, no debug print statements
  • [ ] Commit messages are clear and self-contained — no "AI-generated", "Claude", or tool attribution
  • [ ] make lint-dags passes (or no config/linting.yaml present)
  • [ ] make check passes (schema + operators + secrets + linting + docs)
  • [ ] New linting rules added to config/linting.yaml are documented in docs/userguide/validation-ci.md
  • [ ] make validate output shows correct env class for the test environment

docs.title: 11. Project decisions and trade-offs
docs.text:
Why Go for the generator?

Fast binary, zero Python runtime dependency, straightforward text/template for code generation, easy to embed templates at compile time with go:embed.

Why Go text/template and not a proper AST?

The generated Python is simple and fixed in structure. Template-based generation is easier to read, modify, and review than AST manipulation. The trade-off is that whitespace control requires {{- / -}} discipline.

Why not support sensor operators as standard?

Sensor configuration is highly operator-specific (poke interval, timeout, mode). Rather than guessing a lowest-common-denominator API for each sensor type, we keep the standard list focused on common action operators and let teams register the exact sensor class they need via custom_operators.

Why is _env a shallow merge?

Deep merging nested objects creates unexpected results when a user wants to replace a nested config entirely. Shallow merge is predictable: the entire value is replaced, not patched. For granular overrides, structure your YAML with scalar values that each have their own _env.

Why is there no circular dependency detection?

Adding a graph cycle check at generation time adds complexity but catches a problem that Airflow's own parser already catches at import time with a clear error message. Given that syntax validation (py_compile) already runs after generation, the cycle would be caught before deployment on the very next make generate.

Why is task library expansion non-recursive?

Recursive expansion (library tasks that use other library tasks) creates hard-to-trace resolution chains. The explicit design forces library entries to be self-contained, making their behaviour predictable at the use-site.

Why is parallel generation opt-in at the output handler level (not a CLI flag)?

The Generate() function checks whether the OutputHandler implements Concurrent() bool rather than accepting a --workers flag. This keeps the generator and output packages decoupled. LocalWriter returns true (safe because each goroutine writes a different file). StdoutWriter returns false (serial to keep dry-run output readable and deterministic).

Why is the incremental cache keyed by dag_id rather than input YAML hash?

Keying on the rendered output hash (not the input) means any change that affects the generated Python — template changes, Go binary updates, environment name changes — automatically invalidates the cache. Input-keyed caches would silently skip files after template or generator logic changes.

Why is the linter a separate package rather than part of the validator?

The validator (config/loader.go) enforces structural correctness (required fields, valid types). The linter enforces project conventions (naming patterns, required tags). Separating them makes the linter independently testable and entirely optional — teams can use the generator without ever touching linting.yaml.

docs.title: What is airflow3-dag-gen?
docs.text:
A single-source-of-truth DAG generator for Airflow 3. Your team writes one YAML file; the platform CI generates, validates, and packages the Python DAG files from it automatically.

You never write raw Python DAG files. You write YAML, CI does the rest.

docs.title: 1. Create your first project
docs.text:
Create your project directory and a starter config:

mkdir -p config/projects/<your-team>
touch config/projects/<your-team>/dags.yaml

Open the file and set at minimum:

version: "1.0"        # must match current schema version
name: <your-team>     # used as file prefix in generated output

dags:
  - id: <your-team>_my_first_dag
    schedule: "@daily"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [<your-team>]
    default_args:
      owner: <your-team>
      retries: 1
      retry_delay_minutes: 5
      email_on_failure: false
    tasks:
      - id: hello
        operator: BashOperator
        params:
          bash_command: "echo 'Hello from <your-team>'"

docs.title: 2. Validate locally before pushing
docs.text:
# Check your YAML against the schema (catches typos, wrong types, missing fields)
pip install jsonschema pyyaml
python scripts/validate_configs.py

# Check for hardcoded secrets
python scripts/lint_secrets.py

# Check operator registry compliance
python scripts/validate_operators.py

The same checks run automatically on every PR; fixing them locally saves a round-trip.

docs.title: 3. Understand environment overrides
docs.text:
Every field that should differ between dev, staging, and prod uses the _env key. Fields without _env apply to all environments.

tasks:
  - id: run_job
    operator: BashOperator
    params:
      bash_command: "echo '[dev] light job'"   # used in dev by default
      _env:
        staging:
          bash_command: "echo '[staging] moderate job'"
        prod:
          bash_command: "/opt/scripts/heavy_job.sh"

To disable a DAG or task in a specific environment:

dags:
  - id: expensive_dag
    enabled:
      dev: true
      staging: false   # skipped entirely in staging
      prod: true

docs.title: 4. Preview the resolved config (promotion helper)
docs.text:
Before enabling a DAG in prod, see exactly what will change:

python scripts/promote.py \
  --project <your-team> \
  --from staging \
  --to prod

Output shows which DAGs change, which tasks are added/removed, and which parameters differ between the two environments.

docs.title: 5. Use custom operators
docs.text:
If you need an operator that is not in the standard list, you must:

  1. Register it — open a PR adding an entry to config/operators/registry.yaml:
operators:
  - name: MySpecialOperator
    import_path: plugins.special.MySpecialOperator
    owner: <your-team>
    description: "Does the special thing"
    since: "1.0"
  1. Declare it in your project config:
custom_operators:
  - name: MySpecialOperator
    import_path: plugins.special.MySpecialOperator
  1. Reference it in a task:
tasks:
  - id: special_task
    operator: MySpecialOperator
    params:
      my_param: "value"

The registry PR must be approved by the platform team (@platform-team).

docs.title: 6. Avoid hardcoded secrets
docs.text:
Do not put passwords, tokens, or connection strings directly in YAML:

# BAD — gets flagged by lint_secrets.py and blocked in CI
params:
  password: "super_secret_123"
  db_url: "postgresql://user:pass@host/db"

Do use Airflow Variables or Connections:

# GOOD
params:
  bash_command: "DB_PASSWORD={{ var.value.my_db_password }} python run.py"

docs.title: 7. Standard operators (no registration needed)
docs.text:
These operators are built into the generators and can be used without any registration:

Class name Provider BashOperator core PythonOperator core EmptyOperator core BranchPythonOperator core ShortCircuitOperator core TriggerDagRunOperator core HttpOperator apache-airflow-providers-http BigQueryInsertJobOperator apache-airflow-providers-google SparkSubmitOperator apache-airflow-providers-apache-spark KubernetesPodOperator apache-airflow-providers-cncf-kubernetes PostgresOperator apache-airflow-providers-postgres S3ToRedshiftOperator apache-airflow-providers-amazon

docs.title: 8. What CI does on your PR
docs.text:
Check What it validates Go Tests Generator unit tests pass Python Tests Adapter unit tests pass Lint Python Adapter and scripts code style Validate Config Schema Your YAML matches the JSON schema Validate Operator Registry All custom operators are registered Lint Secrets No hardcoded secrets in configs Backend Parity Test Both backends produce the same DAG IDs

All checks must be green before a PR can be merged.

docs.title: 9. Local generation (optional)
docs.text:
To generate DAG files locally for inspection:

# Install tools
make build

# Generate DAGs
make generate ENV=dev

# Generated files appear in output/dags/

docs.title: 10. Who to contact
docs.text:
• Platform team — schema changes, generator bugs, registry approvals, new standard operators
  • Your team lead — project-level DAG design questions

Check config/operators/registry.yaml for operator ownership. Check .github/CODEOWNERS (when enabled) for file-level review routing.

docs.title: Complete worked example
docs.text:
A production-grade project using project defaults, templates, task library, environment overrides, dynamic mapping, assets, callbacks, and pool control.

version: "1.0"
name: data_platform

defaults:
  max_active_runs: 2
  tags: [data_platform]
  default_args:
    owner: data_team
    retries: 1
    retry_delay_minutes: 10
    email_on_failure: false
    email: oncall@company.com
    _env:
      prod:
        retries: 3
        email_on_failure: true
        execution_timeout_minutes: 90

dag_templates:
  - id: standard_etl
    schedule: "0 3 * * *"
    catchup: false
    pre_tasks:
      - id: check_source
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.common.check_source"
    post_tasks:
      - id: send_notification
        operator: BashOperator
        params:
          bash_command: "echo '{{ pipeline }} complete'"

task_library:
  - id: write_audit
    operator: PythonOperator
    params:
      python_callable: "dags.common.write_audit"
      level: INFO

dags:
  # ── Daily ingest with dynamic mapping ─────────────────────────────────────
  - id: data_platform_ingest
    description: "Ingest events, process each dynamically, publish to asset"
    schedule: "@daily"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    dag_display_name: "Daily Event Ingest"
    doc_md: |
      Fetches events from the API, processes each event in parallel using
      dynamic task mapping, and publishes the result as a Data Asset.
    on_failure_callback: "plugins.alerts.critical_failure"

    enabled:
      dev: true
      staging: true
      prod: true

    tasks:
      - id: fetch_events
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.ingest.fetch_events"
        datasets:
          outlets:
            - uri: "s3://data-platform/raw/events"

      - id: process_event
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.ingest.process_event"
        dynamic_map:
          expand:
            event: "{{ fetch_events.output }}"
          map_index_template: "event_{{ ti.map_index }}"
        pool: processing_pool
        pool_slots: 1
        execution_timeout_minutes: 15
        trigger_rule: all_success
        on_failure_callback: "plugins.alerts.task_failure"
        dependencies: [fetch_events]

      - use: write_audit
        id: audit
        params:
          level: DEBUG
          _env:
            prod:
              level: INFO
        dependencies: [process_event]

  # ── Templated ETL ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - id: data_platform_sales_etl
    template: standard_etl
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    vars:
      pipeline: "sales"
    enabled:
      dev: true
      staging: true
      prod: true
    tasks:
      - id: extract
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.etl.sales.extract"
          _env:
            prod:
              python_callable: "dags.etl.sales.extract_prod"
      - id: transform
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.etl.sales.transform"
        dependencies: [extract]
      - id: load
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.etl.sales.load"
        pool: db_write_pool
        priority_weight: 10
        dependencies: [transform]
    extra_tasks:
      - use: write_audit
        id: sales_audit
        dependencies: [send_notification]

docs.title: Airflow 3.2.2 feature examples
docs.text: Complete dags.yaml DAG definitions for every Airflow 3.x feature supported by the generator, each paired with the Python code that is produced.

docs.title: dag_display_name — human-readable DAG name (Airflow 3.2+)
docs.text:
dag_id must be unique and follow Python identifier conventions. dag_display_name lets you show a friendlier label in the Airflow UI without changing the dag_id.

YAML:

version: "1.0"
name: reporting

dags:
  - id: reporting_weekly_sales_v2
    dag_display_name: "Weekly Sales Report (v2)"
    description: "Generates and distributes the weekly sales summary"
    schedule: "0 6 * * 1"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [reporting, sales]
    default_args:
      owner: data_team
      retries: 2
      retry_delay_minutes: 5
      email_on_failure: true
      email: oncall@company.com
    tasks:
      - id: generate_report
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.reporting.generate_weekly_sales"
      - id: send_report
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.reporting.send_weekly_sales"
        dependencies: [generate_report]

Generated Python (key DAG constructor fields):

with DAG(
    dag_id="reporting_weekly_sales_v2",
    description="Generates and distributes the weekly sales summary",
    schedule="0 6 * * 1",
    start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
    max_active_runs=16,
    tags=["reporting", "sales"],
    default_args=default_args,
    dag_display_name="Weekly Sales Report (v2)",   # ← shown in Airflow UI
) as dag:
    ...

Note

The Airflow UI displays Weekly Sales Report (v2) in the DAG list and detail page. The scheduler, logs, and API still reference reporting_weekly_sales_v2 as the identifier.

docs.title: Asset outlets — publishing data availability (Airflow 3.0+)
docs.text:
Declaring an outlet on a task registers that task as a publisher of a named Asset. Airflow records a data event when the task completes successfully, which can then trigger downstream data-aware DAGs.

YAML:

version: "1.0"
name: ingestion

dags:
  - id: ingestion_daily_events
    description: "Ingest raw events from the API and publish to the data lake"
    schedule: "@daily"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [ingestion]
    default_args:
      owner: data_eng
      retries: 3
      retry_delay_minutes: 10
      email_on_failure: true
      email: data-eng@company.com
    tasks:
      - id: fetch_events
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.ingestion.fetch_events"

      - id: write_to_lake
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.ingestion.write_events_to_lake"
        datasets:
          outlets:
            - uri: "s3://data-lake/events/daily"
        dependencies: [fetch_events]

Generated Python (outlet task):

from airflow.sdk import Asset   # auto-added by generator
from dags.ingestion import fetch_events
from dags.ingestion import write_events_to_lake

with DAG(...) as dag:

    fetch_events = PythonOperator(
        task_id="fetch_events",
        python_callable=fetch_events,
    )

    write_to_lake = PythonOperator(
        task_id="write_to_lake",
        python_callable=write_events_to_lake,
        outlets=[Asset("s3://data-lake/events/daily")],  # ← data event published on success
    )

    fetch_events >> write_to_lake

docs.title: Asset inlets — declaring lineage dependencies (Airflow 3.0+)
docs.text:
inlets annotate a task with the Assets it reads. This is used for lineage tracking in the Airflow UI — it does not affect scheduling.

YAML:

version: "1.0"
name: transform

dags:
  - id: transform_daily_events
    description: "Transform raw events into the analytics schema"
    schedule: "@daily"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [transform]
    default_args:
      owner: data_eng
      retries: 2
      retry_delay_minutes: 5
      email_on_failure: true
    tasks:
      - id: transform_events
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.transform.transform_events"
        datasets:
          inlets:
            - uri: "s3://data-lake/events/daily"
          outlets:
            - uri: "s3://data-lake/events/transformed"

      - id: validate_output
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.transform.validate_output"
        dependencies: [transform_events]

Generated Python (task with both inlet and outlet):

from airflow.sdk import Asset
from dags.transform import transform_events

    transform_events = PythonOperator(
        task_id="transform_events",
        python_callable=transform_events,
        outlets=[Asset("s3://data-lake/events/transformed")],
    )

Note

inlets appear in the Airflow lineage graph but are not emitted as constructor arguments in the current template — they drive UI lineage, not runtime behaviour. outlets are emitted and drive data events.

docs.title: Data-aware scheduling — consumer DAG triggered by Asset (Airflow 3.0+)
docs.text:
A DAG can be scheduled to run whenever a specific Asset is updated, instead of on a time-based schedule. Set schedule to the Asset URI; Airflow 3 resolves it as an Asset trigger.

YAML — producer DAG (publishes the Asset):

version: "1.0"
name: ingestion

dags:
  - id: ingestion_load_customers
    schedule: "0 4 * * *"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [ingestion]
    default_args:
      owner: data_eng
      retries: 2
      retry_delay_minutes: 5
      email_on_failure: true
    tasks:
      - id: load_customers
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.ingestion.load_customers"
        datasets:
          outlets:
            - uri: "s3://data-warehouse/customers/latest"

YAML — consumer DAG (scheduled on the Asset):

version: "1.0"
name: analytics

dags:
  - id: analytics_customer_summary
    description: "Rebuild customer summary table whenever customer data is refreshed"
    schedule: "s3://data-warehouse/customers/latest"   # ← Asset URI as schedule
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [analytics]
    default_args:
      owner: analytics_team
      retries: 1
      retry_delay_minutes: 10
      email_on_failure: true
    tasks:
      - id: rebuild_summary
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.analytics.rebuild_customer_summary"
      - id: refresh_dashboard
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.analytics.refresh_dashboard"
        dependencies: [rebuild_summary]

Generated Python (consumer DAG constructor):

with DAG(
    dag_id="analytics_customer_summary",
    description="Rebuild customer summary table whenever customer data is refreshed",
    schedule="s3://data-warehouse/customers/latest",   # ← Airflow 3 resolves as Asset trigger
    start_date=datetime(2025, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
    ...
) as dag:
    ...

Note

Airflow 3 recognises an Asset URI string as the schedule and triggers this DAG automatically each time ingestion_load_customers completes its load_customers task.

docs.title: Dynamic task mapping with expand (Airflow 3.0+)
docs.text:
Use expand when each mapped task instance receives a single argument that varies. The generator produces .partial().expand().

YAML:

version: "1.0"
name: processing

dags:
  - id: processing_batch_records
    description: "Fetch a list of records and process each one in parallel"
    schedule: "@daily"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [processing]
    default_args:
      owner: data_eng
      retries: 2
      retry_delay_minutes: 5
      email_on_failure: true
    tasks:
      - id: fetch_records
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.processing.fetch_records"

      - id: process_record
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.processing.process_record"
        dynamic_map:
          expand:
            record: "{{ fetch_records.output }}"
        pool: processing_pool
        pool_slots: 1
        execution_timeout_minutes: 10
        on_failure_callback: "plugins.alerts.task_failed"
        dependencies: [fetch_records]

      - id: finalize
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.processing.finalize"
        trigger_rule: all_done
        dependencies: [process_record]

Generated Python:

from dags.processing import fetch_records
from dags.processing import process_record
from dags.processing import finalize
from plugins.alerts import task_failed

    fetch_records = PythonOperator(
        task_id="fetch_records",
        python_callable=fetch_records,
    )

    process_record = PythonOperator.partial(
        task_id="process_record",
        python_callable=process_record,
        pool="processing_pool",
        pool_slots=1,
        execution_timeout=timedelta(minutes=10),
        on_failure_callback=task_failed,
    ).expand(
        record=fetch_records.output,   # ← one task instance per record
    )

    finalize = PythonOperator(
        task_id="finalize",
        python_callable=finalize,
        trigger_rule="all_done",
    )

    fetch_records >> process_record
    process_record >> finalize

docs.title: Dynamic task mapping with expand_kwargs (Airflow 3.0+)
docs.text:
Use expand_kwargs when each mapped task instance receives a dictionary of arguments. The upstream task returns a list of dicts; each dict is unpacked as keyword arguments.

YAML:

version: "1.0"
name: pipeline

dags:
  - id: pipeline_multi_config_jobs
    description: "Run a job for each configuration returned by the config loader"
    schedule: "0 3 * * *"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [pipeline]
    default_args:
      owner: platform_team
      retries: 1
      retry_delay_minutes: 10
      email_on_failure: true
    tasks:
      - id: load_configs
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.pipeline.load_job_configs"

      - id: run_job
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.pipeline.run_job"
        dynamic_map:
          expand_kwargs: "{{ load_configs.output }}"
        execution_timeout_minutes: 30
        dependencies: [load_configs]

      - id: aggregate_results
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.pipeline.aggregate_results"
        dependencies: [run_job]

Generated Python:

from dags.pipeline import load_job_configs
from dags.pipeline import run_job
from dags.pipeline import aggregate_results

    load_configs = PythonOperator(
        task_id="load_configs",
        python_callable=load_job_configs,
    )

    run_job = PythonOperator.partial(
        task_id="run_job",
        python_callable=run_job,
        execution_timeout=timedelta(minutes=30),
    ).expand_kwargs(load_configs.output)   # ← each dict in the list becomes kwargs

    aggregate_results = PythonOperator(
        task_id="aggregate_results",
        python_callable=aggregate_results,
    )

    load_configs >> run_job
    run_job >> aggregate_results

Warning

expand and expand_kwargs are mutually exclusive on a single task. Use expand for a single varying argument; use expand_kwargs when each instance needs a different set of keyword arguments.

docs.title: map_index_template — custom mapped task labels (Airflow 3.0+)
docs.text:
By default Airflow labels mapped task instances as task_id[0], task_id[1], etc. map_index_template lets you set a Jinja expression that produces a meaningful label using task context.

YAML:

version: "1.0"
name: etl

dags:
  - id: etl_regional_pipeline
    description: "Run the ETL pipeline for each region, with labelled task instances"
    schedule: "0 2 * * *"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [etl]
    default_args:
      owner: etl_team
      retries: 2
      retry_delay_minutes: 5
      email_on_failure: true
    tasks:
      - id: get_regions
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.etl.get_active_regions"

      - id: process_region
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.etl.process_region"
        dynamic_map:
          expand:
            region: "{{ get_regions.output }}"
          map_index_template: "region={{ region }}"
        datasets:
          outlets:
            - uri: "s3://data-lake/regions/processed"
        pool: etl_pool
        execution_timeout_minutes: 45
        dependencies: [get_regions]

      - id: merge_regions
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.etl.merge_regions"
        trigger_rule: all_success
        dependencies: [process_region]

Generated Python:

from airflow.sdk import Asset
from dags.etl import get_active_regions
from dags.etl import process_region
from dags.etl import merge_regions

    get_regions = PythonOperator(
        task_id="get_regions",
        python_callable=get_active_regions,
    )

    process_region = PythonOperator.partial(
        task_id="process_region",
        python_callable=process_region,
        outlets=[Asset("s3://data-lake/regions/processed")],
        pool="etl_pool",
        execution_timeout=timedelta(minutes=45),
    ).expand(
        region=get_regions.output,
    )
    process_region.map_index_template = "region={{ region }}"   # ← UI shows "region=eu-west-1" etc.

    merge_regions = PythonOperator(
        task_id="merge_regions",
        python_callable=merge_regions,
        trigger_rule="all_success",
    )

    get_regions >> process_region
    process_region >> merge_regions

Note

The Airflow UI displays each mapped instance as process_region[region=eu-west-1], process_region[region=us-east-1], etc., instead of the default numeric index. The template expression is evaluated at runtime using the task instance context.

docs.title: Comparison: af3-dag-builder vs. Astro DAG Factory
docs.text: Astro DAG Factory is the most widely known YAML-to-DAG tool in the Airflow ecosystem. This page explains the fundamental architectural difference and why af3-dag-builder makes different choices.

docs.title: The core architectural difference
docs.text:
DAG Factory works as a Python library that runs inside Airflow. When the Airflow scheduler scans for DAGs, it imports a loader file that reads your YAML and constructs DAG and operator objects in memory on every scan cycle. There are no generated Python files — the YAML is the only source of truth, interpreted at runtime.

af3-dag-builder works as a compile-time code generator. A Go binary reads your YAML once, resolves environment overrides, and writes real Python .py files to disk. Those files are deployed to Airflow exactly like handwritten DAGs. The generator runs in CI, not in Airflow.

%%{init: {"look": "handDrawn"}}%%
flowchart TB
    subgraph DF["DAG Factory"]
        direction TB
        DF1["dags.yaml"] --> DF2["imported by Airflow scheduler<br/>(every heartbeat)"]
        DF2 --> DF3["DAG objects in memory"]
        DF3 --> DF4["Airflow UI"]
    end

    subgraph AD["af3-dag-builder"]
        direction TB
        AD1["dags.yaml"] --> AD2["make generate<br/>(once, in CI)"]
        AD2 --> AD3["output/dags/project_dag_id.py"]
        AD3 --> AD4["Airflow scheduler"]
    end

docs.title: Feature comparison
docs.text: Capability af3-dag-builder Astro DAG Factory Airflow 3.2.2+ native Built for Airflow 3.x from day one; uses airflow.sdk, airflow.providers.standard.* Built for Airflow 2; Airflow 3 support incomplete Dynamic task mapping (3.0+) .expand() and .expand_kwargs() with YAML syntax; map_index_template supported Not supported for Airflow 3 Airflow 3 Assets (3.0+) Asset inlet/outlet declarations, data-driven scheduling Not supported dag_display_name (3.2+) Set a human-readable name independent of dag_id Not supported Scheduler overhead Zero — DAGs are static .py files YAML parsed and DAGs rebuilt on every scheduler heartbeat Reviewable output Generated .py files committed to git; diffs show exactly what changed No generated files; the runtime behavior is invisible Pre-deployment validation python3 -m py_compile on every file; broken configs never deploy No validation before Airflow loads the file JSON schema validation Full JSON schema (dags.schema.json) checked in CI No schema; YAML errors fail silently at runtime Multi-environment _env overrides on any param; per-env DAG and task enable/disable No built-in environment model Environment promotion diff scripts/promote.py shows the exact param and task delta staging→prod Not provided Secret detection lint_secrets.py blocks hardcoded passwords and tokens in CI Not provided Operator governance Central config/operators/registry.yaml; unknown operators fail CI No registry; typos in operator names fail at runtime DAG templates Reusable DAG skeletons with pre_tasks / post_tasks Not provided Task library Project-level reusable task snippets with use: Not provided Multi-file projects Split large projects across multiple YAML files Not provided Generator performance Compiled Go binary; generates hundreds of DAGs in milliseconds Python interpreted at every scheduler scan Dependency No runtime dependency added to Airflow Adds dag-factory package to Airflow environment

docs.title: When DAG Factory is a reasonable choice
docs.text:
• You are running Airflow 2 with no near-term plan to upgrade.
  • Your team wants the simplest possible setup with no build step.
  • You have only a handful of DAGs and scheduler parse overhead is not a concern.
  • You are already using other Astronomer tooling and want tight integration.

docs.title: When af3-dag-builder is the better fit
docs.text:
• You are on Airflow 3 and need native support for Assets, dynamic task mapping, and other Airflow 3 semantics.
  • You want generated files that your team can read, review in pull requests, and audit — not YAML that only becomes visible inside the Airflow process.
  • You need per-environment configuration discipline: different retries, commands, and enabled states across dev, staging, and prod without duplicating YAML.
  • You run multiple projects in one repo and need a governed operator registry and secret detection as CI gates.
  • Scheduler performance matters: you don't want YAML parsing and DAG object construction happening on every heartbeat.
  • You want a promotion workflow where staging→prod changes are diffed and reviewed before deployment.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
%%{init: {"look": "handDrawn"}}%%
flowchart TD
    A["dags.yaml + sibling *.yaml\n(config/projects/<project>/)"] --> B["Load and merge\ndefaults, task_library,\ntemplates, dag_instances"]
    B --> C["Validate\nids, dependencies,\nduplicates, schema"]
    C --> D["Resolve environment\nenabled_envs, enabled_classes,\nenabled, _env overrides"]
    D --> E["Render dag.py.tmpl"]
    E --> F["output/dags/*.py"]
    F --> G{"output.mode"}
    G -->|local| H["Local filesystem\n(py_compile validated)"]
    G -->|image| I["Docker image\n(+ config/plugins/ if present)"]
  1. You define DAGs in YAML under config/projects/, optionally split across several files, using project defaults, a task library, and DAG templates.
  2. Running make generate (or CI) merges everything, validates it, resolves environment-specific values for the target environment, and renders Python DAG files — one .py per DAG.
  3. Those .py files are deployed to Airflow's dags/ folder (locally) or baked into a Docker image (see Output modes).

Note

You never edit generated files — they are always regenerated from YAML. output/dags/ is gitignored for exactly this reason.

docs.title: Airflow 3.x feature support
docs.text:
The generator targets Apache Airflow 3.2.2 and uses Airflow 3-native APIs throughout:

Feature Airflow version YAML field(s) airflow.providers.standard.* operator paths 3.0+ all built-in operators from airflow.sdk import Asset 3.0+ datasets.outlets / datasets.inlets Asset-driven data-aware scheduling 3.0+ datasets.outlets .partial().expand() dynamic task mapping 3.0+ dynamic_map.expand .partial().expand_kwargs() 3.0+ dynamic_map.expand_kwargs map_index_template on mapped tasks 3.0+ dynamic_map.map_index_template dag_display_name 3.2+ dag_display_name

docs.title: Custom operators
docs.text:
Use an operator that is not in the standard list:

Step 1 — register in the global registry (requires platform team approval):

# config/operators/registry.yaml
operators:
  - name: MySpecialOperator
    import_path: plugins.special_ops.MySpecialOperator
    owner: my_team
    description: "Does the special thing"
    since: "1.0"

Step 2 — declare in your project config:

custom_operators:
  - name: MySpecialOperator
    import_path: "plugins.special_ops.MySpecialOperator"

Step 3 — use in a task:

tasks:
  - id: special_task
    operator: MySpecialOperator
    params:
      config_key: "value"
      threshold: 0.95

The generator resolves the import and produces:

from plugins.special_ops import MySpecialOperator

special_task = MySpecialOperator(
    task_id="special_task",
    config_key="value",
    threshold=0.95,
)

docs.title: Callbacks
docs.text:
Callbacks are Python callables defined in your plugins/ or dags/ directory, referenced by their full dotted import path. The generator automatically adds the required from ... import ... statement.

DAG-level:

dags:
  - id: critical_pipeline
    on_failure_callback: "plugins.alerts.send_pagerduty_alert"
    on_success_callback: "plugins.metrics.record_dag_success"
    on_sla_miss_callback: "plugins.alerts.send_sla_warning"
    ...

Task-level:

tasks:
  - id: risky_task
    operator: PythonOperator
    on_failure_callback: "plugins.alerts.task_failed"
    on_retry_callback: "plugins.alerts.task_retrying"
    params:
      python_callable: "dags.pipeline.risky_step"

Generated Python:

from plugins.alerts import send_pagerduty_alert
from plugins.alerts import task_failed
from plugins.alerts import task_retrying

with DAG(
    ...,
    on_failure_callback=send_pagerduty_alert,
) as dag:
    risky_task = PythonOperator(
        ...,
        on_failure_callback=task_failed,
        on_retry_callback=task_retrying,
    )

Note

Callback import path format: module.submodule.function_name — the last dot-segment is the function name; everything before it is the module path.
