docs.title: Environment overrides
docs.text:
Any scalar field under params or default_args can be overridden per environment using the _env key. The base value is the fallback for environments not explicitly listed.

tasks:
  - id: run_job
    operator: BashOperator
    params:
      bash_command: "echo dev run"      # used in dev (and any unlisted env)
      workers: 1
      _env:
        staging:
          bash_command: "echo staging run"
          workers: 4
        prod:
          bash_command: "/opt/scripts/prod_run.sh"
          workers: 16

Effective params after resolution, per environment:

devstagingprod 
bash_command: "echo dev run"
workers: 1

bash_command: "echo staging run"
workers: 4

bash_command: "/opt/scripts/prod_run.sh"
workers: 16

Enable/disable a DAG per environment:

dags:
  - id: expensive_dag
    enabled:
      dev: true
      staging: false    # skipped in staging; not generated at all
      prod: true

Enable/disable a task per environment:

tasks:
  - id: debug_task
    operator: BashOperator
    enabled:
      dev: true
      staging: false
      prod: false       # task removed; its dependents' upstream edges are cleaned up
    params:
      bash_command: "echo debug"

Full resolution order (this is the complete picture — it's what actually runs, in order, for every DAG on every generation):

%%{init: {"look": "handDrawn"}}%%
flowchart TD
    A["DAG"] --> B{"enabled_envs set\nand env not listed?"}
    B -->|yes| X["DAG excluded\n(not generated at all)"]
    B -->|no| C{"enabled_classes set\nand class not listed?"}
    C -->|yes| X
    C -->|no| D{"enabled[env] == false?"}
    D -->|yes| X
    D -->|no / unset| E["Merge default_args._env[env]"]
    E --> F["Merge DAG-level _env[env]\nschedule, catchup, max_active_runs, tags"]
    F --> G["Per task: drop if enabled[env]==false,\nclean dangling dependency edges,\nmerge params._env[env]"]
    G --> H["Resolved DAG -> rendered to output/dags/*.py"]
  1. enabled_envs whitelist (if set, the active env must be in the list)
  2. enabled_classes whitelist (if set, the active env's class must be in the list)
  3. DAG enabled[env] == false → entire DAG skipped
  4. default_args._env[env] merged onto base default_args
  5. DAG-level _env[env] merged (schedule, catchup, max_active_runs, tags)
  6. Per task: enabled[env] == false → task omitted and downstream dependency edges cleaned; params._env[env] merged onto base params and the _env key removed from output

docs.title: Environment taxonomy and classes
docs.text:
By default the generator recognises three built-in environment names and maps them to a class:

Environment name(s) Class prod, prd, production production staging, stg staging anything else (e.g. dev, qa) non-production

You can replace this with an explicit taxonomy in config/settings.yaml:

solution: custom
environment: prd-eu

environments:
  prd-eu:
    label: "Production EU"
    class: production
  prd-us:
    label: "Production US"
    class: production
  stg:
    label: "Staging"
    class: staging
  dev:
    label: "Development"
    class: non-production

Note

Once defined, the class is used by enabled_classes filtering and shown in make validate output.

docs.title: DAG-level _env overrides
docs.text:
In addition to params._env and default_args._env, you can override DAG-level scheduling fields per environment using _env at the DAG level:

dags:
  - id: heavy_pipeline
    schedule: "@daily"
    catchup: false
    max_active_runs: 1
    tags: [team_a]

    _env:
      prod:
        schedule: "0 3 * * *"    # tighter cron in prod
        max_active_runs: 2        # allow more concurrency in prod
      staging:
        tags: [team_a, staging]   # add extra tag in staging

Fields supported in a DAG-level _env block:

Field Description schedule Override the cron / preset schedule catchup Override the catchup flag max_active_runs Override the maximum concurrent runs tags Replace the entire tags list

Note

Only non-null values in the override block are applied; unset fields keep their base value.

docs.title: enabled_envs and enabled_classes
docs.text:
Two whitelist fields give you precise control over which environments a DAG is generated for, without maintaining a per-env enabled map.

enabled_envs — list of environment names:

dags:
  - id: mock_data_loader
    schedule: "@hourly"
    enabled_envs: [dev, qa]   # only generated in dev and qa; skipped in staging and prod
    ...

enabled_classes — list of environment classes:

dags:
  - id: integration_test_dag
    schedule: "@daily"
    enabled_classes: [non-production]   # generated in dev and staging; never in prod
    ...

Comparison:

Mechanism Key question Example use case enabled: {prod: false} Is this specific env explicitly disabled? One-off exclusion enabled_envs: [dev] Is the active env in this whitelist? Dev-only tooling enabled_classes: [non-production] Does the active env's class match? All non-prod envs regardless of name

Note

Resolution order: enabled_envs is checked first, then enabled_classes, then enabled. All must pass for the DAG to be generated.

docs.title: Previewing and applying environment diffs
docs.text:
Before promoting a DAG from staging to prod, check exactly what will change:

python scripts/promote.py \
  --project my_team \
  --from staging \
  --to prod

Output shows which DAGs change, which tasks are added/removed, and which parameters differ between the two environments.

docs.title: Generating an apply patch
docs.text:
Once you've reviewed the diff and decided which changes to backfill, use --apply to generate the minimal _env.{to_env} YAML stanza:

# Print to stdout
python scripts/promote.py --project my_team --from staging --to prod --apply

# Write to a file for review
python scripts/promote.py --project my_team --from staging --to prod --apply --output patch.yaml

The output is a ready-to-paste YAML block. Copy the relevant sections into your dags.yaml, run make validate, then commit.

# Makefile shortcut
make promote-apply PROJECT=my_team FROM=staging TO=prod

Warning

--apply shows field-level changes only. DAGs that are entirely enabled or disabled in one environment (but not the other) still require manual enabled configuration.

docs.title: FAQ & Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Q: My DAG isn't appearing in Airflow after generation. Check: (1) the generated .py file exists in output/dags/; (2) make validate passes; (3) the DAG is not disabled for the target environment via enabled.

Q: I get a "unknown operator" error. Either the operator isn't in the standard list (see Operators & Callbacks) or it's missing from custom_operators in your project config. If it's a new custom operator, it also needs to be registered in config/operators/registry.yaml.

Q: How do I run a DAG only in prod?

enabled:
  dev: false
  staging: false
  prod: true

Q: Can I reference Airflow Variables or Connections in params? Yes — use Jinja templating exactly as you would in native Python DAGs:

params:
  bash_command: "echo {{ var.value.my_variable }}"
  conn_id: "{{ conn.my_connection.conn_id }}"

Q: What happens if I disable a task that other tasks depend on? Dependency edges pointing to the disabled task are automatically removed from all downstream tasks. No manual cleanup needed.

Q: How do I generate for multiple environments? Run make generate once per environment:

make generate ENV=dev
make generate ENV=staging
make generate ENV=prod

Q: Can I see what changed between environments before deploying? Yes — use the promotion helper:

python scripts/promote.py --project my_project --from staging --to prod

Q: How do I create 20 identical DAGs with different parameters?

Use dag_instances to stamp out N DAGs from one template without repeating the full DAG block each time:

dag_templates:
  - id: my_template
    tasks: [...]

dag_instances:
  - id: my_dag_us
    template: my_template
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    vars: { region: us }
  - id: my_dag_eu
    template: my_template
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    vars: { region: eu }

Q: How do I make a DAG only appear in non-production environments (dev, staging) regardless of their names?

Use enabled_classes:

enabled_classes: [non-production]

This works even as you add new non-production environment names (e.g. qa, perf) — no config changes needed.

Q: How do I see what _env overrides to add to close the gap between staging and prod?

python scripts/promote.py --project my_project --from staging --to prod --apply

This prints a YAML patch you can paste directly into your dags.yaml.

Q: How do I speed up generation for a large project?

Generation already runs py_compile in parallel (one goroutine per CPU). For CI re-runs on mostly-unchanged configs, add --incremental:

daggen --settings config/settings.yaml --incremental

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Get a working DAG generated and running in Airflow in under five minutes. No Python or Go knowledge is required — you write YAML, the platform does the rest.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Tool Minimum version Purpose Apache Airflow 3.2.2 Target runtime — all generated DAGs target this version make any Run all developer commands Go 1.22+ Build the Go generator Python 3.10+ Syntax validation and config validation scripts Docker any Local Airflow 3.2.2 test environment

Airflow version requirement

Generated DAGs use from airflow.sdk import Asset, airflow.providers.standard.* module paths, and the dag_display_name parameter — all of which require Airflow 3.x. The dag_display_name field specifically requires 3.2+. The project is not compatible with Airflow 2.x.

Install the build tools and Python dependencies:

make build

docs.title: Creating your first project
docs.text:
Step 1 — create your project directory:

mkdir -p config/projects/my_team
touch config/projects/my_team/dags.yaml

Step 2 — edit the file. At minimum set name and one DAG:

version: "1.0"
name: my_team

dags:
  - id: my_team_hello
    schedule: "@daily"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    catchup: false
    tags: [my_team]
    default_args:
      owner: my_team
      retries: 1
      retry_delay_minutes: 5
      email_on_failure: false
    tasks:
      - id: hello
        operator: BashOperator
        params:
          bash_command: "echo hello"

Step 3 — validate:

make validate

Step 4 — generate and inspect:

make generate ENV=dev
cat output/dags/my_team_my_team_hello.py

Step 5 — smoke-test in local Airflow:

make airflow-up
# open http://localhost:8080  (admin / admin)
make airflow-down

Next steps

Once this works: the YAML Reference has the full field list, Templates & Reuse covers stamping out many similar DAGs, and the FAQ covers the most common stumbling blocks.

docs.title: DAG templates
docs.text: Templates let you define a reusable DAG skeleton and stamp out multiple instances.

docs.title: Partial template (most common)
docs.text:
Define pre_tasks and/or post_tasks. Each instance provides its own core tasks.

dag_templates:
  - id: standard_etl
    schedule: "0 2 * * *"
    catchup: false
    default_args:
      retries: 2
      email_on_failure: true
    pre_tasks:
      - id: validate_source
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.common.validate_source"
    post_tasks:
      - id: notify
        operator: BashOperator
        params:
          bash_command: "echo '{{ pipeline_module }} complete'"

dags:
  - id: sales_etl
    template: standard_etl
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    vars:
      pipeline_module: "dags.sales"
    tasks:                           # core tasks between pre and post
      - id: extract
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.sales.extract"
      - id: load
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.sales.load"
        dependencies: [extract]
    extra_tasks:                     # appended after post_tasks
      - id: audit
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.sales.audit"
        dependencies: [notify]

Final task order: validate_source → extract → load → notify → audit

%%{init: {"look": "handDrawn"}}%%
flowchart LR
    A["pre_tasks\n(template)"] --> B["tasks\n(instance's own core tasks)"]
    B --> C["post_tasks\n(template)"]
    C --> D["extra_tasks\n(instance only)"]

Template fields only fill gaps left at their zero value

catchup, email_on_failure, and similar plain (non-_env) fields work by "the DAG's own value wins if it's not the zero value, otherwise the template's value is used" — and Go can't tell "explicitly set to false" apart from "not set at all" for a plain bool. So a template with catchup: true cannot be overridden back to catchup: false by an instance's dags: entry, because false looks identical to "unset" to the merge logic. The same applies to default_args.email_on_failure: false overriding a template default of true. If you need a DAG to opt out of a template's true default, use a DAG-level _env override instead (pointer-typed fields can distinguish "set to false" from "unset"), or use dag_instances — its Catchup field is nullable and doesn't have this limitation.

docs.title: Full template
docs.text:
Define tasks inside the template. Instances cannot add core tasks (only extra_tasks).

dag_templates:
  - id: full_report
    tasks:
      - id: generate
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "{{ report_module }}.generate"
      - id: upload
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "{{ report_module }}.upload"
        dependencies: [generate]

dags:
  - id: weekly_report
    template: full_report
    vars:
      report_module: "dags.reports.weekly"
    start_date: "2025-01-01"

docs.title: Variable substitution
docs.text:
Use {{ var_name }} in task params values and task ids. Values come from the DAG's vars block.

vars:
  pipeline_module: "dags.sales"
  environment_name: "production"

docs.title: dag_instances — compact bulk instantiation
docs.text:
When you need to stamp out many structurally identical DAGs from the same template, dag_instances is more concise than repeating individual dags: entries with template:. Each entry in dag_instances expands to one DAG using the named template.

dag_templates:
  - id: regional_etl
    schedule: "0 3 * * *"
    catchup: false
    default_args:
      owner: data_eng
      retries: 2
      retry_delay_minutes: 10
      email_on_failure: true
    tasks:
      - id: extract
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.etl.{{ region }}.extract"
      - id: load
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.etl.{{ region }}.load"
        dependencies: [extract]

dag_instances:
  - id: etl_us_east
    template: regional_etl
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    vars:
      region: us_east

  - id: etl_eu_west
    template: regional_etl
    start_date: "2025-01-01"
    vars:
      region: eu_west
    tags: [eu, etl]               # instance-specific overrides are allowed
    schedule: "0 5 * * *"         # different schedule for this instance

  - id: etl_ap_south
    template: regional_etl
    start_date: "2025-06-01"
    vars:
      region: ap_south
    enabled_classes: [production]  # this instance only generated in prod environments

Note

dag_instances entries are expanded before project defaults are applied, so defaults.tags, defaults.max_active_runs, and defaults.default_args all apply uniformly.

Fields available on each dag_instances entry:

dag_instances has full field parity with plain dags: entries — anything you can set on a DAG, you can set (or override from the template) on an instance.

Field Description id Required. Unique DAG ID template Required. ID of a dag_templates entry start_date Required. DAG start date (YYYY-MM-DD) vars Template variable substitutions ({{ var }} in task params) description Short description shown in the Airflow UI DAG list schedule Override the template's schedule catchup Override the template's catchup flag max_active_runs Override the template's max_active_runs end_date Override the DAG's end date (YYYY-MM-DD) tags Override the template's tags group Output sub-directory enabled Per-env enable/disable map enabled_envs Env name whitelist enabled_classes Env class whitelist _env DAG-level per-env overrides (schedule, catchup, etc.) default_args Override default_args for this instance datasets Asset outlets/inlets — see Asset outlets and inlets doc_md Markdown documentation rendered in the Airflow UI DAG detail view dag_display_name Human-readable display name (Airflow 3.2+) render_template_as_native_obj Render Jinja-templated fields as native Python objects on_failure_callback / on_success_callback / on_sla_miss_callback DAG-level lifecycle callbacks — see Operators & Callbacks extra_tasks Additional tasks appended after all template tasks

docs.title: Task library
docs.text:
Define reusable task snippets once, reference them in any DAG with use:.

task_library:
  - id: log_completion
    operator: BashOperator
    params:
      bash_command: "echo pipeline complete"

  - id: write_audit
    operator: PythonOperator
    params:
      python_callable: "dags.common.write_audit_log"
      level: INFO

dags:
  - id: my_dag
    tasks:
      - id: extract
        operator: PythonOperator
        params:
          python_callable: "dags.pipeline.extract"

      - use: log_completion         # copies library entry
        id: done                    # override the id
        dependencies: [extract]     # add edges; library deps are also inherited

      - use: write_audit
        id: audit
        params:
          level: DEBUG              # override a single param; others keep library values
        dependencies: [done]

Note

Override rules: task-site fields win over library fields. params are merged key-by-key (site wins on conflict).

docs.title: Multi-file projects
docs.text:
A project directory can contain multiple YAML files. This is useful for separating DAG definitions into logical groups.

Layout:

config/projects/my_project/
├── defaults.yaml      ← primary file (metadata: name, version, defaults, templates, task_library)
├── etl_dags.yaml      ← extra file (adds dags, custom_operators, task_library)
└── reporting_dags.yaml ← extra file

Rules:

  • If defaults.yaml is present it is loaded first as the primary file.
  • If only dags.yaml exists it is the primary file.
  • All other *.yaml files in the directory are merged alphabetically.
  • Extra files may contain: dags, custom_operators, dag_templates, task_library.
  • Fields from the primary file (name, version, defaults) are not overridden by extra files.

Note

make validate (schema, operator registry, and secret checks) covers every *.yaml file in the project directory, not just the primary file — the same merged view the Go generator uses. Split freely without losing validation coverage on the sibling files.

Primary file example (defaults.yaml):

version: "1.0"
name: my_project

defaults:
  max_active_runs: 2
  tags: [my_project]
  default_args:
    owner: my_team
    retries: 1

dag_templates:
  - id: standard_etl
    ...

task_library:
  - id: audit_log
    ...

Extra file example (etl_dags.yaml):

dags:
  - id: my_project_daily_etl
    schedule: "@daily"
    ...

docs.title: daggen CLI flags
docs.text:
make generate, make validate, etc. are thin wrappers around the daggen binary. All flags are optional and can be combined:

Flag Purpose --settings <path> Path to settings.yaml (default config/settings.yaml) --env <name> Override the environment from settings.yaml for this run only --project <name> Generate/validate only the named project instead of every project under config/projects/ --validate Check configs and print a report; writes nothing --dry-run Render DAGs and print the Python source to stdout instead of writing files --incremental Skip DAGs unchanged since the last run (see Incremental generation) --manifest Write manifest.json after generation (see DAG manifest) --output-dir <path> Override the output directory from settings.yaml (useful in CI) --base-dir <path> Repository root used for auto-discovering config/projects/ (default .)

Use case — inspect one DAG's generated Python without writing any files:

app/dagGen/bin/daggen --settings config/settings.yaml --project my_team --dry-run

This is the fastest way to check "what will this actually render to?" while iterating on a template or a tricky _env override, without touching output/dags/ or running a full make generate.

Use case — validate or generate a single project in a large monorepo:

app/dagGen/bin/daggen --settings config/settings.yaml --project ecommerce_platform --validate

docs.title: Local (default)
docs.text:
Generated .py files are written to the filesystem:

# config/settings.yaml
output:
  mode: local
  local:
    path: ./output/dags

make generate ENV=prod
ls output/dags/

docs.title: Docker image
docs.text:
Generated files are baked into a Docker image based on the Airflow base image:

output:
  mode: image
  image:
    name: airflow-dags
    tag: "1.0.0"
    base_image: apache/airflow:3.2.2
    push: true
    registry: myregistry.example.com

make generate ENV=prod
# Builds and optionally pushes: myregistry.example.com/airflow-dags:1.0.0

Plugins are bundled automatically

If config/plugins/ exists and is non-empty, it's copied into the build context and COPY'd to /opt/airflow/plugins/ alongside the DAGs — no extra config needed. The Generate and Package DAGs CI workflow does the same for the local-mode artifact zip: generated DAGs land under dags/ and, when present, plugins land under plugins/, so the artifact is deployable as-is.

docs.title: Validation and linting
docs.text:
Run all validators locally before pushing:

make validate

This runs three checks:

Check Command What it catches Schema validation python scripts/validate_configs.py Wrong field types, missing required fields, invalid patterns Operator registry python scripts/validate_operators.py Custom operators used in configs but not registered in registry.yaml Secret detection python scripts/lint_secrets.py Hardcoded passwords, tokens, connection strings

Note

All three checks (and scripts/promote.py) validate every *.yaml file in a project directory — the same merged view the Go generator uses for multi-file projects — not just dags.yaml or defaults.yaml.

Do not hardcode secrets in YAML:

# BAD — flagged and blocked in CI
params:
  password: "hunter2"
  db_url: "postgresql://user:pass@host/db"

# GOOD — use Airflow Variables or Connections
params:
  bash_command: "DB_PASS={{ var.value.my_db_password }} python run.py"

docs.title: Generator-level safety checks
docs.text:
Beyond JSON schema validation, the Go generator itself (daggen, run by make generate / make validate) rejects configs that would otherwise fail silently or unsafely at Airflow parse time:

Check Rejects DAG/task id character allowlist Any id not matching ^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$ — ids are emitted as bare Python identifiers, so this also closes a code-injection gap if daggen is ever run without the separate validate-schema step group path safety group segments that don't match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$ (blocks path-traversal values like ../../etc that would otherwise be joined into the output file path) Duplicate task ids Two tasks with the same id inside one DAG Dangling / self dependencies A task's dependencies entry that doesn't match any task id in the same DAG, or a task depending on itself Duplicate collection ids Two entries with the same id in custom_operators, task_library, or dag_templates output.image.base_image newline injection A base_image value containing a newline (would otherwise inject arbitrary Dockerfile instructions) Malformed dates start_date / end_date values that aren't valid calendar dates (e.g. 2024-13-45) even if they match the YYYY-MM-DD shape

Note

These run as part of make validate and make generate — you don't need a separate command. They catch mistakes that used to only surface as an Airflow DAG-parse error or, in the id/path cases, as a security gap.

docs.title: Naming convention linting
docs.text:
If config/linting.yaml exists, the generator checks DAG IDs, task IDs, tags, and descriptions against the rules you define. Violations cause --validate and make lint-dags to exit with a non-zero status.

config/linting.yaml example:

rules:
  dag_id:
    pattern: "^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$"
    message: "DAG IDs must be lowercase snake_case"
  task_id:
    pattern: "^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$"
    message: "Task IDs must be lowercase snake_case"
  required_tags:
    - team
  description_required: true

Supported rules:

Rule key Type Description dag_id.pattern regex string DAG IDs that don't match exit 1 task_id.pattern regex string Task IDs that don't match exit 1 required_tags list of string Every DAG must carry all listed tags description_required boolean Every DAG must have a non-empty description

Note

Linting is entirely opt-in — delete or rename linting.yaml to disable it. The make check target runs make lint-dags as part of the full CI gate.

make lint-dags    # validate + linting only
make check        # schema + operators + secrets + linting + docs

docs.title: Incremental generation
docs.text:
Pass --incremental to skip regenerating DAGs whose content hasn't changed since the last run. The generator writes a .daggen-cache.json hash file to the output directory and compares SHA-256 hashes on subsequent runs.

# First run — generates all DAGs and writes cache
daggen --settings config/settings.yaml --incremental

# Second run — unchanged DAGs are skipped (shown as "↩ … (unchanged)")
daggen --settings config/settings.yaml --incremental

When to use it:

Scenario Benefit Large repo (500+ DAGs) in CI Skip py_compile for unchanged files; typical CI re-run goes from 30s → 3s Local iteration on one project Only re-generates the project you edited Post-merge sync Unchanged DAGs stay in place; only changed projects regenerate

The cache is keyed by dag_id. Changing the environment name or any YAML that affects the rendered output will cause a regeneration. Delete .daggen-cache.json to force a full regeneration.

docs.title: DAG manifest
docs.text:
Pass --manifest to write a manifest.json file alongside the generated .py files. The manifest lists every DAG that was generated for the active environment.

make generate ENV=prod
daggen --settings config/settings.yaml --manifest
# → output/dags/manifest.json

manifest.json structure:

{
  "generated_at": "2025-06-17T12:00:00Z",
  "environment": "prod",
  "env_class": "production",
  "solution": "custom",
  "git_commit": "a1b2c3d",
  "dag_count": 42,
  "dags": [
    {
      "id": "my_dag",
      "project": "my_project",
      "file": "my_dag.py",
      "group": "",
      "schedule": "@daily",
      "start_date": "2025-01-01",
      "catchup": false,
      "max_active_runs": 1,
      "tags": ["team_a", "prod"],
      "task_count": 5
    }
  ]
}

Use cases:

  • Feed a governance dashboard with the active DAG inventory per environment
  • Diff manifests across environments to see what runs where
  • Use dag_count in CI as a sanity check (alert if it drops unexpectedly)
  • Drive operator/tag coverage reports

docs.title: Project-level fields
docs.text:
version: "1.0"          # required; must be "1.0"
name: my_project        # required; alphanumeric + hyphens/underscores; used as filename prefix

defaults:               # applied to every DAG unless overridden at DAG level
  max_active_runs: 1
  tags: [team_tag]
  group: etl            # default output sub-directory
  default_args:
    owner: my_team
    retries: 1
    retry_delay_minutes: 5
    email_on_failure: false

custom_operators:       # non-standard operators used in this project
  - name: MyOp
    import_path: "plugins.my_module.MyOp"
    description: "optional description"

task_library:           # reusable task snippets — see Templates & Reuse
  - id: log_done
    operator: BashOperator
    params:
      bash_command: "echo done"

dag_templates:          # reusable DAG patterns — see Templates & Reuse
  - id: standard_etl
    schedule: "0 2 * * *"
    pre_tasks: [...]
    post_tasks: [...]

dags:                   # required; at least one DAG
  - ...

docs.title: DAG fields
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description id string yes Unique DAG identifier; alphanumeric and underscores only description string no Short description shown in the Airflow UI DAG list schedule string no Cron expression (e.g. 0 2 * * *) or preset (@daily, @hourly, @weekly, @monthly) start_date string no DAG start date in YYYY-MM-DD format end_date string no Optional end date; no new runs are scheduled after this date (YYYY-MM-DD) catchup boolean no Backfill missed intervals between start_date and today on first deploy (default: false) max_active_runs integer ≥1 no Maximum number of concurrent DAG runs (default: 16) group string no Output sub-directory for this DAG (overrides project default) tags list of string no UI filter tags; merged with project-level tags (deduped) enabled_envs list of string no Whitelist of environment names; DAG is only generated when the active environment appears in this list. Absence of this field means all environments are allowed. enabled_classes list of string no Whitelist of environment classes (e.g. non-production, staging, production); DAG is only generated when the active environment's class appears in this list. Use this instead of enabled_envs when you want env-name independence. _env object no Per-environment overrides for DAG-level scheduling fields (schedule, catchup, max_active_runs, tags). Keys are environment names; values are the fields to override. doc_md string no Markdown documentation rendered in the Airflow UI DAG detail view dag_display_name string no Human-readable display name shown in the Airflow 3.2+ UI (overrides dag_id) render_template_as_native_obj boolean no When true, Jinja-templated fields are rendered as native Python objects instead of strings on_failure_callback string no Dotted import path to a callable invoked when the DAG fails (e.g. plugins.alerts.notify) on_success_callback string no Dotted import path to a callable invoked when the DAG succeeds on_sla_miss_callback string no Dotted import path to a callable invoked on SLA miss

Note

enabled, default_args, tasks, extra_tasks, template, vars, and datasets are structural fields covered in dedicated sections below.

docs.title: Task fields
docs.text:
Field Type Required Description id string no Unique task identifier within the DAG; alphanumeric and underscores only use string no Reference to a task_library entry id; library fields are merged as defaults operator string no Operator class name — standard built-in or registered custom operator doc string no Task-level documentation shown in the Airflow UI task detail view dependencies list of string no List of upstream task ids; generates upstream >> this_task edges trigger_rule string no Rule determining when this task is triggered relative to its upstream tasks — all_success, all_failed, all_done, all_skipped, one_success, one_failed, one_done, none_failed, none_skipped, none_failed_min_one_success, always, dummy pool string no Airflow pool name used to limit concurrency for this task pool_slots integer ≥1 no Number of pool slots this task occupies (default: 1) queue string no Celery/Kubernetes queue this task is submitted to priority_weight integer ≥1 no Task priority — higher values run first when the pool/executor has capacity weight_rule string no Algorithm for computing effective priority_weight across the DAG — downstream, upstream, absolute, exponential execution_timeout_minutes integer ≥1 no Maximum runtime in minutes before the task instance is killed and marked failed sla_minutes integer ≥1 no Expected maximum duration in minutes; triggers on_sla_miss_callback when exceeded on_failure_callback string no Dotted import path to a callable invoked when this task fails on_success_callback string no Dotted import path to a callable invoked when this task succeeds on_retry_callback string no Dotted import path to a callable invoked when this task is retried

Note

params, enabled, dynamic_map, and datasets are covered in dedicated sections below.

trigger_rule values:

Value Meaning all_success (default) All upstream tasks succeeded all_failed All upstream tasks failed all_done All upstream tasks finished (any state) all_skipped All upstream tasks were skipped one_success At least one upstream task succeeded one_failed At least one upstream task failed one_done At least one upstream task finished none_failed No upstream task failed or upstream-failed none_skipped No upstream task was skipped none_failed_min_one_success None failed and at least one succeeded always Run regardless of upstream state dummy Deprecated alias for always

Example — task with scheduling fields:

- id: critical_load
  operator: PythonOperator
  params:
    python_callable: "dags.etl.load"
  trigger_rule: all_done
  pool: db_pool
  pool_slots: 2
  queue: high_memory
  priority_weight: 10
  execution_timeout_minutes: 30
  sla_minutes: 45
  on_failure_callback: "plugins.alerts.pagerduty_alert"
  dependencies: [transform]

docs.title: Callable resolution: python_callable and callbacks
docs.text:
python_callable (in params) and every on_*_callback field share one mechanism: you write a dotted path — module.submodule.function_name — and the generator:

  1. Splits it at the last dot into a module (module.submodule) and a name (function_name).
  2. Emits from module.submodule import function_name once at the top of the file (deduplicated even if several tasks import different names from the same module).
  3. References the bare function_name at the call site — never the full dotted path.

So python_callable: "dags.pipeline.process_record" becomes:

from dags.pipeline import process_record
...
python_callable=process_record,   # not dags.pipeline.process_record

The path must contain at least one dot

A value with no dot (e.g. python_callable: "process_record") has nothing to split into a module — the generator silently skips the import and emits the bare name as-is. Because this is a name-resolution problem, not a syntax error, it passes python3 -m py_compile and make validate and only fails as NameError: name 'process_record' is not defined when Airflow actually parses the DAG. Always use a fully-qualified module.function path.

Avoid a task id that matches its own callable's function name

If a task's id is identical to the imported function's name (e.g. id: process_record calling python_callable: "dags.pipeline.process_record"), the generated line process_record = PythonOperator(..., python_callable=process_record) reassigns process_record from the imported function to the operator object. That single line still works (Python evaluates the right-hand side first), but if a later task in the same file also needs process_record as a python_callable, it would now resolve to the operator instance instead of the function. Give the task a different id from its callable's function name if the same function is reused elsewhere in the DAG.

docs.title: default_args fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description owner string Task owner displayed in the Airflow UI retries integer ≥0 Number of automatic retries before the task is marked as failed retry_delay_minutes integer ≥0 Wait time in minutes between retry attempts email_on_failure boolean Send an email alert when a task instance fails email string or list of string Email address or list of addresses for failure/retry alerts email_on_retry boolean Send email on task retry (default: true in Airflow) depends_on_past boolean Task only runs if the previous run of the same task succeeded execution_timeout_minutes integer ≥1 Maximum runtime per task instance in minutes before it times out

Note

Use _env inside default_args to override any of these fields per environment — see Environments.

default_args:
  owner: data_team
  retries: 2
  retry_delay_minutes: 10
  email_on_failure: true
  email:
    - oncall@company.com
    - team@company.com
  email_on_retry: false
  depends_on_past: false
  execution_timeout_minutes: 60
  _env:
    prod:
      retries: 5
      execution_timeout_minutes: 120

docs.title: Dynamic task mapping (requires Airflow 3.0+)
docs.text:
Generates Airflow 3's .partial().expand() or .partial().expand_kwargs() pattern. The map_index_template field requires Airflow 3.0+.

expand — map over individual arguments:

- id: process_record
  operator: PythonOperator
  params:
    python_callable: "dags.pipeline.process_record"
  dynamic_map:
    expand:
      record: "{{ fetch_records.output }}"   # raw Python expression
    map_index_template: "record_{{ ti.map_index }}"
  dependencies: [fetch_records]

Generated Python: 

from dags.pipeline import process_record   # auto-added — see note below

process_record = PythonOperator.partial(
    task_id="process_record",
    python_callable=process_record,
).expand(
    record=fetch_records.output,
)
process_record.map_index_template = "record_{{ ti.map_index }}"

expand_kwargs — map over a list of dicts:

- id: run_job
  operator: PythonOperator
  params:
    python_callable: "dags.pipeline.run_job"
  dynamic_map:
    expand_kwargs: "{{ get_job_configs.output }}"
  dependencies: [get_job_configs]

Generated Python: 

from dags.pipeline import run_job

run_job = PythonOperator.partial(
    task_id="run_job",
    python_callable=run_job,
).expand_kwargs(get_job_configs.output)

Warning

expand and expand_kwargs are mutually exclusive — use one per task.

docs.title: Asset outlets and inlets (requires Airflow 3.0+)
docs.text:
Declare Airflow 3 Asset dependencies to enable data-driven DAG scheduling. Assets replace the Airflow 2.x Dataset concept — the generator emits from airflow.sdk import Asset automatically when any task declares outlets or inlets.

tasks:
  - id: produce_report
    operator: PythonOperator
    params:
      python_callable: "dags.reporting.produce"
    datasets:
      outlets:
        - uri: "s3://reports-bucket/daily/report.csv"
      inlets:
        - uri: "s3://source-bucket/raw/events.json"

Generated Python: 

from airflow.sdk import Asset          # auto-added when outlets/inlets are present
from dags.reporting import produce     # auto-added — see note below

produce_report = PythonOperator(
    task_id="produce_report",
    python_callable=produce,
    outlets=[Asset("s3://reports-bucket/daily/report.csv")],
)

Note

inlets are declared on the task for lineage tracking. outlets additionally drive data-aware scheduling — a downstream DAG that declares schedule: <asset-uri> will be triggered automatically when this task completes.
